newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ ELECTION - Reserve Bank, labour market policies.
newsitem.headline: NZ ELECTION - Reserve Bank, labour market policies.

text.p: Here is a summary of how New Zealand's main political parties stand on the Reserve Bank Act and the Employment Contracts Act, key pillars of the country's free-market reforms.
New Zealanders vote on Saturday in their first general election under a new system of proportional representation which favours coalition or minority governments.
RESERVE BANK ACT
The RBA, introduced in 1989 by the then Labour government, created an autonomous central bank whose governor is bound by contract to pursue price stability.

The bank currently has a 0-2 percent target band for underlying inflation, but this is not legislated, and can be changed at any time by agreement between the finance minister and the governor of the Reserve Bank.

The outgoing conservative NATIONAL party government and its potential coalition partners on the right and centre-right -- ACT NEW ZEALAND, the CHRISTIAN COALITION and UNITED -- are all committed to the 0-2 percent target band and the central bank's single objective of price stability.

LABOUR believes the target band is too narrow and would widen it to minus one to three percent pending a review of the correct measure of price stability. It does not favour broadening the central bank's objectives.

NEW ZEALAND FIRST wants to expand the Reserve Bank's objectives to include sustainable economic growth, and require it to target inflation at a rate below the average of New Zealand's major trading partners.
The ALLIANCE would widen the goals to include employment and "sustainable well being", and drop the 0-2 percent target band, replacing it with the goal of price stability over the economic cycle.
EMPLOYMENT CONTRACTS ACT

NATIONAL remains committed to the 1991 Employment Contracts Act, which bans strikes and lockouts related to multi-employer contracts. Employees and employers can bargain individually or collectively. Closed shops are outlawed. Personal grievance provisions and access to specialist Employment Court for all employees. In practice, the Act has sharply curbed the power of trade unions.
Other parties' policies are as follows:
ACT
-- Favours status quo but would review need for a specialist Employment Court.
ALLIANCE
-- Repeal act.
-- Return to collective bargaining with national and industry-wide contracts. Strikes and lockouts would be lawful.
-- Require negotiations in good faith.
-- Provide four weeks' annual leave and 12 weeks paid parental leave
-- Boost minimum wage to $7.50 an hour from $6.375.
CHRISTIAN COALITION
-- Supports "broad thrust" of Employment Contracts Act, but would review it to ensure the rights and responsibilities of employers and employees were fairly balanced.
LABOUR
-- Replace ECA with Employment Relations Act.
-- Require negotiations in good faith.
-- Provide six weeks' paid parental leave.
-- Apply International Labour Organisation principles of free worker association and collective bargaining, but workers would have right to sign individual contracts.
-- Right to strike protected by law.
-- Comprehensive minimum code.
-- New Employment Relations Commission to provide mediation service.
-- Boost minimum wage for workers 18 and over to $7.35/hour.
NEW ZEALAND FIRST
-- Amend rather than repeal the ECA to make it "fairer" and require bargaining in good faith.
-- Bring all employment-related law, including holidays and health and safety, within the ECA.
-- Compulsory arbitration for essential services.
-- Raise minimum wage to $7.50/hour for people 20 and over and proportionately less for teenagers.
-- Include new provisions requiring good faith bargaining, and "reasonable access" to workplaces for bargaining agents.
UNITED
-- Retain the ECA.
